analogy.p: Think of a torch (the centre of enlargement) shining a hand shape onto a wall. Moving the hand closer to the torch makes a smaller shadow (scale factor less than 1), and moving it further away makes a bigger one. If you put the screen behind the torch so the picture appears the other way up on the opposite side, that is like a negative scale factor. The analogy breaks down because a real shadow projection is limited by how far the screen is, whereas a mathematical enlargement can be any size and the centre can be anywhere.
analogy.t: A shadow puppet and a projector

bullets: **Translation:** described by a column vector; the shape moves without turning or changing size.
**Reflection:** described by the equation of the mirror line, for example x = 2, y = -1, y = x or y = -x.
**Rotation:** described by the angle, the direction (clockwise or anticlockwise) and the centre of rotation.
**Enlargement:** described by the scale factor and the centre of enlargement; scale factors can be whole, fractional or negative.
**Combinations:** you may be asked to describe a single transformation equivalent to two done in a row.
Describing a transformation 'fully' means giving **all** the required details; marks are lost if one is missing.
Only enlargement changes the size; translations, reflections and rotations produce **congruent** images.
core.p: Edexcel Higher asks you to **describe and transform shapes using translations, reflections, rotations and enlargements**, including enlargements with **fractional and negative scale factors**. You must be able to carry out a transformation on a grid, describe a given transformation **fully** using the correct mathematical language, and use combinations of transformations. At Higher you are also expected to find the **centre of enlargement** or **centre of rotation** when it is not given, and to link enlargement to area and volume scale factors. These questions are worth 2 to 4 marks and appear on all three papers.

bullets: **Congruent** images: translation, reflection and rotation (lengths, angles and area unchanged).
**Similar** images: enlargement (angles unchanged, lengths multiplied by k, areas by k²).
**Orientation** (the way round the shape faces) changes under reflection (the shape is flipped) but not under translation, rotation or enlargement with positive k.
The image is often labelled with a **dash** such as A' (read 'A prime') for the point A.
A point that does not move under the transformation is an **invariant point** (for example any point on the mirror line in a reflection, or the centre of a rotation).
A line is an **invariant line** if every point on it is mapped to a point on that line.
Corresponding vertices are labelled in order, so draw the image carefully point by point.
core.p: The original shape is called the **object** and the shape after the transformation is the **image**. Under a translation, reflection or rotation the image is **congruent** to the object, meaning the same size and shape, with the same side lengths and angles. Under an enlargement the image is **similar** to the object: the angles stay the same, but lengths change by the scale factor. Knowing which properties are preserved helps you to check answers and to choose the right type of transformation.

bullets: The vector (3 over -2) means **3 right and 2 down**.
Top number = horizontal movement (x); bottom number = vertical movement (y). Right and up are positive.
To find the vector, count from a vertex of the object to the **same vertex** of the image.
The **inverse** of the translation by (a over b) is the translation by (-a over -b).
Translating by (2 over 1) then by (3 over -4) is the same as one translation by the **sum** (5 over -3).
When describing a translation you must give **the word 'translation' and the vector**; do not give a direction in words alone.
Vectors can be written in bold letters or with an arrow in diagrams; a is the vector from one point to another.
core.p: A **translation** moves every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction. It is described by a **column vector** written (x over y), where x is the movement to the right (negative means left) and y is the movement up (negative means down). Under a translation the shape does not turn, flip or change size. To translate a shape, apply the vector to every vertex; to describe a translation, find the movement from one vertex to its image.

bullets: Vertical mirror lines have equations **x = a**; horizontal lines have equations **y = b**.
The **x-axis** is y = 0 and the **y-axis** is x = 0.
Diagonal mirror lines: **y = x** and **y = -x**; for these, turn the paper or use the coordinate rules.
**Coordinate rules:** reflect in x-axis (x, y) goes to (x, -y); in y-axis (x, y) goes to (-x, y); in y = x (x, y) goes to (y, x); in y = -x (x, y) goes to (-y, -x).
Points **on the mirror line** do not move (they are invariant).
For a diagonal mirror line, measure distances **at right angles to the line**, not horizontally or vertically.
To **find the mirror line**, join a point to its image, find the midpoint, and draw the perpendicular through it (the perpendicular bisector).
Describe it as: **Reflection in the line x = ...** (never just 'it flips').
core.p: A **reflection** flips a shape over a **mirror line** so that each point and its image are the **same perpendicular distance** from the mirror line on opposite sides. The mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of the line joining a point to its image. To reflect a shape, count the perpendicular distance of each vertex from the mirror line and plot the image the same distance on the other side. To describe a reflection you must give the **equation of the mirror line**.

bullets: **Angle:** commonly 90°, 180° or 270°; 90° clockwise is the same as 270° anticlockwise.
**Direction:** clockwise (like a clock's hands) or anticlockwise.
**Centre:** the coordinates of the fixed point, for example (0, 0) or (2, -1).
**Rules about the origin:** 90° anticlockwise (x, y) goes to (-y, x); 90° clockwise goes to (y, -x); 180° goes to (-x, -y).
To **carry out** a rotation, you may use tracing paper: trace the shape, pin the centre and turn.
To **find the centre**, draw the perpendicular bisectors of the lines joining two pairs of corresponding points; they meet at the centre.
The centre is the only point that does not move (the **invariant point**).
State the transformation fully: **Rotation, 90° anticlockwise, centre (0, 0).**
core.p: A **rotation** turns a shape about a fixed point called the **centre of rotation** through a given angle in a given direction. The distance of each point from the centre stays the same, and the image is congruent to the object. To describe a rotation you must give **three things**: the **angle**, the **direction** (clockwise or anticlockwise) and the **centre**. For 180° the direction does not matter because it is the same either way.

bullets: **Scale factor = image length ÷ object length.**
Scale factor greater than 1 gives a **bigger** image; scale factor between 0 and 1 gives a **smaller** image (a **reduction**).
The distance from the centre is multiplied by the scale factor: a vertex 3 units from the centre moves to 6 units for k = 2.
From the origin: (x, y) goes to (kx, ky).
About any centre (a, b): image = centre + k × (point - centre); do the vector from the centre first.
Method: draw a **ray** from the centre through each vertex, mark the new point at k times the distance, and join the points.
If the centre is **inside** the shape or on the shape, the image overlaps the object.
To **describe** an enlargement, give: **enlargement, scale factor, centre**.
core.p: An **enlargement** changes the size of a shape by a **scale factor** from a **centre of enlargement**. Every length is multiplied by the scale factor, but the angles do not change, so the image is **similar** to the object. To enlarge a shape, draw a line from the centre through each vertex and extend it so that the distance from the centre to the image vertex is (scale factor) times the distance from the centre to the object vertex. Then join the image vertices. The **position** of the image depends on the centre, so you must always state it.

bullets: Scale factor **1/2:** every length is halved and the image is half as far from the centre as the object.
Scale factor **1/3:** each image point is one third of the way from the centre.
**Area** of the image = original area × k², for example k = 1/2 gives area ÷ 4.
If the image is smaller than the object, the scale factor is **less than 1** but still positive.
To **find** a fractional scale factor, divide a length of the image by the corresponding length of the object.
Using a **reciprocal**: if A goes to B with scale factor 2 from centre O, then B goes back to A with scale factor 1/2 from O (the inverse).
Example: vertex (8, 6) enlarged scale factor 1/2 from centre (4, 2): the vector from the centre is (4, 4), half is (2, 2), the image is (6, 4).
core.p: A fractional scale factor between 0 and 1 produces a **smaller** image, although the transformation is still called an enlargement. The same method applies: the image vertices are found a fraction of the way from the centre to each object vertex. For example, scale factor 1/2 means each image point is **halfway** between the centre and the object point. Fractional enlargements are very common at Higher because they test whether you have understood that 'enlargement' means any change in size.

bullets: **|k|** gives the size change; the **negative sign** gives the opposite side of the centre.
About the origin: (x, y) goes to (kx, ky) with k negative, so scale factor -2 gives (-2x, -2y).
Scale factor **-1** is the same as a **rotation of 180°** about the centre of enlargement.
The image is **upside down** relative to the object, but not reflected (orientation of the vertex order is preserved).
**Draw rays through the centre** past it to the other side; measure the distance (|k| times the distance from the centre).
Example: triangle (1,1), (3,1), (1,2) with scale factor -2 from (0,0) goes to (-2,-2), (-6,-2), (-2,-4).
Area still changes by **k²** (positive): scale factor -2 multiplies area by 4.
To **describe**, say 'enlargement, scale factor -2, centre (0, 0)'; a describing mark is lost if the sign is missing.
core.p: A **negative scale factor** puts the image on the **opposite side of the centre** from the object, and the image is **inverted** (turned upside down, like a 180° rotation combined with a size change). The size of the image is given by the **modulus** of the scale factor: a scale factor of -2 makes lengths twice as long, and -1/2 makes them half as long. Every image point lies on the line through the object point and the centre, but on the other side. This is a Higher tier topic and it is often tested with a grid and coordinates.

bullets: Draw **at least two lines** through corresponding vertices; check a third passes through the same point.
If the lines meet **between** the object and the image, the scale factor is **negative**; if the object and image are on the same side of the meeting point, it is positive.
**Scale factor** = image length ÷ object length (use a pair of corresponding sides).
The answer format is: **Enlargement, scale factor ..., centre (..., ...)**.
If the shape is on a grid, count the squares to get coordinates of the centre.
A scale factor of 1 would be no change, so if the shapes are the same size check for another transformation.
For a mixed question 'describe the single transformation that maps A to B', look first at size (enlargement?), then orientation (reflection?), then position.
core.h: Finding the centre of enlargement and describing fully
core.p: When the centre is not given, you can find it by drawing a straight line through each pair of **corresponding vertices** (an object vertex and its image vertex) and extending the lines until they meet. The point where they all meet is the **centre of enlargement**. Then find the scale factor by dividing an image length by the matching object length, and decide whether the sign is positive (image on the same side of the centre as the object) or negative (opposite side). Always **give all three parts** in the answer.

bullets: Two reflections in **parallel** mirror lines give a **translation** (twice the distance between the lines, perpendicular to them).
Two reflections in **perpendicular** lines through the origin give a **rotation of 180°** about the origin.
Reflection in the y-axis then reflection in the x-axis: (x, y) goes to (-x, y) then to (-x, -y), a **180° rotation**.
Two translations: add the vectors.
**Inverse of a translation** by a vector: translation by the negative vector.
**Inverse of a reflection:** the same reflection.
**Inverse of a rotation:** rotation by the same angle in the opposite direction about the same centre.
**Inverse of an enlargement** with scale factor k: enlargement with scale factor 1/k from the same centre.
core.p: Two transformations performed one after the other are called a **combined transformation**. Often the result can be described as a **single transformation**, for example a reflection followed by another reflection in a perpendicular line is a rotation of 180°. Order can matter: translate then reflect is usually different from reflect then translate. The **inverse** of a transformation undoes it. Practising with a grid and tracing paper helps to see these results.

bullets: Scale factor 3: lengths x3, area x9, volume x27.
Scale factor -2: lengths x2 (and inverted), area x4.
Scale factor 1/2: lengths ÷2, area ÷4, volume ÷8.
Perimeter changes by |k|; area by k².
The **angles** of the shape do not change under any enlargement.
Shapes related by an enlargement are **similar**, and their corresponding sides are parallel.
Because area changes by k² you can find k from the area ratio: area ratio 9 : 1 means |k| = 3.
core.p: Enlargement links directly to the topic of **similar shapes and area and volume scale factors**. If the linear scale factor is k (positive or negative) then lengths are multiplied by |k|, areas by **k²** and volumes by **k³** in magnitude. A negative scale factor does not make area negative: area scale factor is always positive because (-2)² = 4. This connection means that a question can ask you to find the area of an enlarged shape without drawing it.

bullets: **Plot** the image one vertex at a time and check by counting squares.
Mark the **centre** and draw construction rays for an enlargement.
Use **tracing paper** for rotations to check the direction and angle.
For a mirror line, check by **folding** or by comparing distances at right angles.
Write the **type** first: translation, reflection, rotation or enlargement; then the details.
If asked for a single transformation, **do not** give two answers.
In 'describe fully' questions, one missing detail (for example the centre) usually loses marks.
State the scale factor as a **fraction or negative** if appropriate.
core.h: Exam technique and common question types
core.p: Transformations questions are usually 2 to 4 marks. Marks are for carrying out the transformation accurately (shape in correct position) or for stating every required detail. Use a ruler, pencil and, if allowed, tracing paper. Draw construction lines lightly so the examiner can see your method. When describing, read the command word: 'describe **fully**' means the type plus all details; 'describe the **single** transformation' means do not give a combination.

exam: **Command words:** 'describe fully' needs every detail; 'describe the single transformation' needs one transformation; 'enlarge' or 'reflect' needs an accurate drawing.
**Marks:** translate/reflect/rotate on a grid is usually 2 marks (1 mark for correct orientation or 3 correct vertices, 1 for full accuracy); describing is usually 2 to 3 marks (1 per detail).
**Describe a translation:** 'Translation by the vector (a over b)' using the correct signs.
**Describe a reflection:** 'Reflection in the line y = ...' or 'x = ...'; a diagonal line needs y = x or y = -x.
**Describe a rotation:** 'Rotation, 90° anticlockwise, centre (0, 0)' with all three details.
**Describe an enlargement:** 'Enlargement, scale factor 2, centre (1, 3)' and include the sign for a negative scale factor.
Draw **construction lines lightly** (rays from the centre, perpendicular bisectors) so that method marks can be given.
Use a **sharp pencil and ruler**; image vertices should be accurate to within half a square.
To find a **centre of rotation**, draw two perpendicular bisectors; to find a **centre of enlargement**, draw lines through corresponding vertices.
Check your **final shape**: same size for translation, reflection, rotation; scaled for enlargement; and ask whether it is the right way round.
For **combined transformations**, apply them in the order given and label the shapes (A to B to C) to avoid mixing them up.

mistakes.r: Give all three: angle, direction (clockwise or anticlockwise) and centre of rotation.
mistakes.w: Describing a rotation without the centre or the direction (e.g. 'rotate 90°').

mistakes.r: Write 'reflection in the line x = 2' (or y = ..., y = x, y = -x) with the correct equation.
mistakes.w: Describing a reflection as 'flip' or giving a direction instead of the mirror line.

mistakes.r: Write 'enlargement, scale factor 2, centre (0, 0)': scale factor and centre are both required.
mistakes.w: Describing an enlargement without the centre, or with only a scale factor.

mistakes.r: Give one transformation only: if the question says describe fully, give the type plus all required details in one answer.
mistakes.w: Using two or more transformations when the question says 'a single transformation'.

mistakes.r: Top number is horizontal (right positive), bottom is vertical (up positive): 3 right, 2 down is (3 over -2).
mistakes.w: Putting the translation vector the wrong way round (y over x) or ignoring negative signs.

mistakes.r: Measure perpendicular (at right angles) to the mirror line, or use the rule (x, y) goes to (y, x) for y = x.
mistakes.w: Measuring the distance to a diagonal mirror line horizontally or vertically.

mistakes.r: A negative scale factor puts the image on the opposite side of the centre, inverted.
mistakes.w: Putting the image on the same side of the centre for a negative scale factor.

mistakes.r: Measure every distance from the centre of enlargement, not from the object's nearest vertex.
mistakes.w: Enlarging by counting squares from the shape instead of from the centre of enlargement.

mistakes.r: Area scales by k²: scale factor 1/2 gives an area one quarter as big.
mistakes.w: Thinking scale factor 1/2 makes the area half as big.

mistakes.r: Use tracing paper and check: anticlockwise is the opposite way to clock hands; 90° clockwise = 270° anticlockwise.
mistakes.w: Rotating in the wrong direction because clockwise and anticlockwise are mixed up.

summary: Edexcel Higher asks you to carry out and fully describe translations (vectors), reflections (mirror lines), rotations (angle, direction, centre) and enlargements, including fractional and negative scale factors, and to find a centre of enlargement or rotation. It matters because describe-fully questions need every detail for full marks and enlargement links to area and volume scale factors.

terms.d: A change in the position, orientation or size of a shape: translation, reflection, rotation or enlargement.
The object is the original shape; the image is the shape after the transformation.
A transformation that moves every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction, described by a column vector.
A pair of numbers written one above the other showing the horizontal movement (top) and vertical movement (bottom).
A transformation that flips a shape in a mirror line so each point and its image are the same perpendicular distance from the line.
The line in which a shape is reflected; it is the perpendicular bisector of each point and its image.
A transformation that turns a shape through a given angle in a given direction about a fixed point.
The fixed point about which a shape is turned; it does not move.
A transformation that changes the size of a shape by a scale factor from a centre, keeping the shape the same.
The number by which every length is multiplied in an enlargement: image length ÷ object length.
The fixed point from which an enlargement is made; image points lie on rays through it.
An enlargement in which the image is on the opposite side of the centre and inverted; size change is the modulus of the scale factor.
Having exactly the same shape and size; the image of a translation, reflection or rotation is congruent to the object.
Having the same shape but a different size; the image of an enlargement is similar to the object.
A point that does not move under a transformation, for example the centre of a rotation.
A line at right angles to a line segment through its midpoint; used to find mirror lines and centres of rotation.
The two directions of turning: the same way as the hands of a clock, or the opposite way.

worked.ans: Image vertices (-2, -2), (-6, -2), (-2, -4); area 4 square units. The image is on the opposite side of the origin and inverted.
worked.q: Triangle T has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1) and (1, 2). Enlarge T by scale factor -2 with centre (0, 0). Write down the coordinates of the vertices of the image and the area of the image. [3 marks]
steps: Multiply each coordinate by -2 (centre is the origin): (1, 1) goes to (-2, -2). [M1]
Area scale factor = (-2)² = 4, so image area = 4 square units. [B1]
Check: image base from (-2,-2) to (-6,-2) is 4, height from y = -2 to y = -4 is 2, so area = 1/2 × 4 × 2 = 4. ✓

worked.q: Triangle A has vertices (4, 4), (8, 4) and (4, 6). Enlarge A by scale factor 1/2 with centre (2, 2). [3 marks]
steps: Find the vector from the centre to each vertex: (4,4) gives (2, 2); (8,4) gives (6, 2); (4,6) gives (2, 4). [M1]
Check: the image base is 5 - 3 = 2, half of the original base 8 - 4 = 4. ✓

worked.q: Triangle P has vertices (1, 2), (1, 4) and (3, 2). Triangle Q has vertices (-2, 1), (-4, 1) and (-2, 3). Describe fully the single transformation that maps P to Q. [3 marks]
steps: Q is the same size as P, so it is not an enlargement; it is congruent. The orientation is the same, so it is a rotation (not a reflection).
Test the rule for 90° anticlockwise about the origin: (x, y) goes to (-y, x). Then (1, 2) goes to (-2, 1) ✓; (1, 4) goes to (-4, 1) ✓; (3, 2) goes to (-2, 3) ✓. [M1]
So the angle is 90° and the direction is anticlockwise. [A1]
The centre is the origin (0, 0), as the rule was applied about (0, 0). [A1]
